Each finished track writes a field into a Redis hash keyed by match and segment number, and the muxer proceeds only when the field count equals the configured track total — and only if that segment isn't already in a "done" set, so a duplicate delivery can't mux the same segment twice.

The consequence is the honest tradeoff of the design: the slowest language sets the latency for everybody. Adding a sixth language cannot make the output faster and can easily make it slower. That's the price of shipping one stream with every track in it rather than one stream per language.

Buffering: why four segments, not one

The receiver doesn't publish a segment the moment it lands. It holds a rolling window of four segments and publishes them together, and the transcriber transcribes the whole window but keeps only the words belonging to the middle segment.

This is a deliberate accuracy-for-latency trade. Speech recognition is much worse at a hard cut — a word split across a segment boundary is a word it gets wrong, and football commentary is full of names it can only resolve from surrounding context. Giving it roughly twenty-four seconds of continuous audio and then trusting only the centre means every word is transcribed with real context on both sides. The cost is paid once, in fixed delay, rather than continuously in mistranscribed names.

Failure behaviour

Every stage is separated from the next by a topic, so a stage that dies comes back and resumes from its committed offset rather than losing the backlog. A rules failure doesn't kill the consumer: the original message is republished to that service's retry topic and the loop continues, so one malformed segment cannot wedge a language lane.

Segment numbering survives restarts through Redis — the receiver reads the last media sequence back on startup and continues from it, instead of restarting at zero and producing a playlist that jumps backwards.

Delivery has its own health notion. The processes that re-encapsulate the output for each broadcaster parse their own encoder progress, and exit deliberately when throughput drops below three-quarters of the expected frame rate, letting the container restart policy rebuild the connection. A stalled-but-alive encoder is worse than a dead one, because nothing downstream notices.

Configuration as the unit of change

Almost every processor is the same container image. A translator and a speech synthesiser differ by the rules file and config mounted into them, not by their runtime. Config is loaded into Redis at startup and read from there, so a running service can be repointed without a rebuild, and the set of live services is inspectable because each one registers itself and cleans up its own keys on shutdown.

Adding a language is therefore a directory, two topics and a compose entry — no new program.

Three things hang off the side

Beyond the dubbing path, the same material feeds three services that the live pipeline never waits on.

Highlight reels come from a branch reading the same receiver topic as the transcriber, sharing nothing else with it. It accumulates a much longer window, sends the stitched video to a video-understanding model to find goals and near-misses, has a second model re-check the result to throw out false positives, and uploads what survives. Because it is a separate consumer group it can fall behind, fail, or be switched off entirely and the dubbing pipeline never notices — which is exactly why it hangs off a topic rather than being bolted into the transcriber.

A full-match highlights cut is assembled on request from the clips that branch produced, concatenated in order with a broadcast bumper spliced onto both ends.

Match reports are the neatest reuse in the project. The report service takes the subtitles the pipeline has already produced as its source, feeds the stitched commentary to a language model, and writes a written match report from it — then translates that report into ten languages. The live path's byproduct becomes another product's raw material at no extra cost to it.

Its one genuinely clever step is proper-noun correction. Speech recognition reliably mangles player names, and a match report full of misspelt footballers is worthless. So the model is handed a search-grounded squad list for the fixture and told to correct names against it before writing — repairing upstream transcription errors at the point where they would actually be noticed, rather than trying to make the recogniser perfect.
SDE.lld:
Keeping subtitles on the video

This is the part that looks trivial and isn't. Subtitles are published per segment, but a player needs to know where a segment's cue times sit on the video's timeline, not on a timeline starting at zero.

MPEG-TS timestamps run on a 90 kHz clock — 90 ticks per millisecond. Each subtitle file is written with cue times relative to its own segment, plus a header line anchoring local zero to that segment's real presentation timestamp:

  • X-TIMESTAMP-MAP=LOCAL:00:00:00.000,MPEGTS:<start_ms × 90>

For that anchor to be true, the original timestamps have to survive every single media operation in the pipeline. Which is why -copyts and -mpegts_copyts 1 appear on every encoder invocation — segmenting, audio extraction, speech alignment, muxing. Miss them once and that stage helpfully resets timestamps to zero, the anchor becomes a lie, and subtitles drift against the picture in a way that looks like a subtitle bug but is actually a muxing bug several stages upstream.

The full journey of one timestamp: source PTS → preserved through segmentation → read back out with a probe in milliseconds → carried on the Kafka message → added to the word offsets the recogniser returns → subtracted again to make cue times segment-relative → multiplied by 90 to write the anchor.

Making a translation fit the time it has

A sentence translated into another language is a different length, and a dub has a fixed slot: the segment it belongs to. Overrun and either the audio is cut off or it walks into the next segment.

The Hindi lane is the one built out furthest, and handles this in three stages:

  • Translate in a commentary register — native script, but keeping the English football loanwords commentators actually say rather than "correct" translations nobody uses.
  • Predict the spoken duration before synthesising it, using a small regression model trained on text features. If the prediction overruns the English source by more than a couple of seconds, the text is sent back to be compressed — rewritten shorter against a syllables-per-second budget. This is the interesting bit: it fixes length before spending an API call, rather than generating audio and discovering it doesn't fit.
  • Tag for delivery — emotion markers the voice model understands, chosen from match intensity measured as a rolling words-per-second window, with recent context read back so the same tag isn't repeated every segment.

The other four lanes are single-stage translation and take the simpler route: if the synthesised audio overruns, it is sped up with a filter, capped at 1.2× so it never becomes a chipmunk.

Stitching speech into a fixed slot

Synthesised phrases don't add up to exactly one segment. The gaps between them are adjustable and the segment length is not, so the audio is assembled in two passes: first absorbing any carry-over left by the previous segment, then shrinking the silences if the total still overruns. Anything that still doesn't fit becomes carry-over for the next segment — with a hard cap, because an uncapped carry-over is a slow drift that gets worse for the whole match.

The synthetic commentary is mixed against the real stadium audio rather than replacing it: crowd noise ducked, commentary lifted. Losing the stadium is what makes a dub feel like a voiceover instead of a broadcast.

Output and delivery

The final stage writes the media playlist, the per-language subtitle playlists and a master playlist advertising the audio and subtitle tracks. Segment durations are measured with a probe rather than assumed, because a playlist whose declared durations don't match its segments desynchronises players slowly.

Every playlist write is atomic — written to a temporary file, flushed, then renamed over the target. Players poll these files constantly, and a non-atomic write means eventually serving a half-written playlist to somebody.

From there the output is served over HTTP by a small nginx cluster and separately re-encapsulated to SRT per broadcaster. The cache policy splits the two kinds of file: playlists are explicitly uncacheable because they change every few seconds, while the video segments are immutable once written and cached hard. Getting that backwards is either a stale-playlist bug or a pointless origin hammering.

Adaptors

A set of small single-purpose services around the edges: protocol conversion into and out of the pipeline, and a time-shifted output that republishes the playlist a fixed number of segments behind live. The delay is done by rewriting sequence numbers, which is cheap and correct as long as segments are uniform — and they are, because the segmenter forces keyframes at segment boundaries.

What I would change

  • The barrier has no timeout — one permanently stuck language lane stalls output for every language. It should degrade to shipping the tracks that are ready and backfill, rather than blocking.
  • Two copies of the logic exist: the built image and the volume-mounted runtime copy that overrides it. Convenient for hot-fixing mid-match, but the two drift and the running copy is the only one that's true.
  • Several long-running services rely on the container restart policy rather than their own recovery loop — restart-as-error-handling works until the thing that failed is the restart.
  • Encoder settings are nominally variable bitrate but set to identical target and maximum, so they are constant bitrate with extra steps.
  • Credentials sit inline in service configs; they belong in injected secrets.

SDE.name: Sports Intelligence Console
SDE.description: The control plane for the multilingual streaming pipeline. Operators create a match from a form and the backend generates a whole per-match pipeline stack from templates — stream-scoped Kafka topics, processor configs, compose file — then runs and supervises it. Replaced a workflow that needed a developer on the server.
highlights: Built the control plane that replaced hand-operated streaming deployments: operators create a match from a form and the backend generates a complete per-match pipeline stack from templates, then runs and supervises it.

Designed stream-scoped naming for Kafka topics, consumer groups, processor directories and containers so multiple matches run concurrently on shared infrastructure without consuming each other’s segments.
Derived the entire inter-service wiring contract from a single language list, replacing ~50 hand-typed topic literals whose only guarantee of agreement was that the same string had been typed twice.
Split pipeline creation from execution across two endpoints so a misconfiguration produces an inspectable file rather than a half-started stack, and matches can be prepared well ahead of kickoff.
Added role-based access, token refresh with enforced password expiry, and live container stats and log streaming over sockets — removing SSH from the day-to-day operating loop.
SDE.overview:
The streaming pipeline used to be operated by hand. Running a match meant a developer on the server: editing config files, wiring Kafka topic names so services could find each other, bringing containers up in the right order, and tailing logs over SSH when something stalled. One match at a time, and only by someone who knew the whole system.

This console is what replaced that. An operator fills in a form — who's producing the feed, which fixture, what protocol comes in, which outputs go out — and the backend generates an entire pipeline stack from templates and runs it. No file editing, no SSH, and no requirement that the person running the match be the person who built the pipeline.

The key move is templatisation. The pipeline stopped being a hand-maintained deployment and became a shape that gets stamped out per match, so several matches can run side by side without their services colliding.

  • Create a match from a form; the backend writes a per-stream compose file and a full tree of processor configs
  • Run, stop, restart individual services from the browser, with live logs and container stats streamed back
  • Three roles — admin, developer, viewer — so operating a match no longer requires the keys to everything
  • Clients modelled properly — agency, tournament, match — instead of living in someone's config file

The console never touches a video frame. It is a code generator and a process supervisor; the actual transcoding, translation and dubbing happen in the pipeline it starts.
SDE.hld:
The console has one job that matters and it is not the UI: it turns a form submission into a set of files on disk that constitute a working pipeline, then hands them to Docker. Everything else — auth, roles, clients, log streaming — exists to make that job safe to hand to someone who isn't a developer.

Generation is separate from execution

Creating a stream and running one are two different requests. Create validates the input, renders templates, rewrites configs and writes a compose file — and stops. Nothing is started. A second, explicit call brings the stack up.

That split is worth the extra step. Generation is the part that can be wrong in interesting ways, and separating it means a bad config produces a bad file you can read rather than a half-started stack you have to tear down. It also makes creating a match well ahead of kickoff a normal thing to do — the stack sits on disk, generated and inspectable, until someone presses run.

Why every match needs its own names

The services in the pipeline find each other purely by Kafka topic and consumer-group name. There is no service discovery: a translator knows its input because a string in its config says so.

That makes the naming convention the entire wiring contract — and it means two concurrent matches using the same names would silently consume each other's segments. So every generated stack gets stream-scoped names: the topics, the consumer groups, the processor directories and the container names all carry the stream id. Isolation comes from the naming scheme rather than from separate infrastructure, which is what allows several matches to share one Kafka cluster.

There's a nice piece of engineering history in that file. The naming used to be roughly fifty hand-typed template literals across a config table — the same topic name written six times, a translator and its speech service sharing a consumer group only because the identical string had been typed twice. It's now derived from a single list of languages, so adding a language touches one array and the folder names cannot drift from the config table. That's the difference between a convention and a contract.

Supervising something that isn't yours

The console shells out to the host Docker CLI rather than driving a Docker library. The containers it starts are therefore siblings on the host daemon, not children of the backend — which has a consequence that is the single most common way this system breaks.

The backend writes compose files at a path inside its own container, but the bind-mount strings baked into those files have to be host paths, because the daemon resolving them lives on the host. Two different path roots for the same directory. If they drift apart the generated pipeline starts perfectly and mounts empty directories — the worst failure shape available, because nothing errors.

Access, and why roles were the point

The original workflow had exactly one privilege level: shell access to the server. The console splits that into admin, developer and viewer, so someone can watch a match run without being able to delete it.

Auth is a short-lived access token with a refresh token in an httpOnly cookie, and password expiry is enforced as middleware — an expired password blocks every route except changing it, rather than being a warning the UI could skip.

Live feedback

Container stats are pushed to the browser on an interval over a socket, and log streams are subscribed per stream. This is the part that replaced tailing files over SSH, and it is why the console can be the only place an operator needs to look.

Infrastructure health — broker, cache, proxy, the transcription hosts — is polled and shown as a strip across the top, because "is my match broken or is the cluster broken" was previously a question only a developer could answer.
SDE.lld:
What one "create" actually produces

A create request runs three generators over the same validated config:

  • Template copy — the runtime templates for receivers, processors and senders are copied into a stream-scoped directory, with generic folder names rewritten to carry the stream id, so hindi-translator becomes hindi-translator-<id>.
  • Config rewrite — every processor's config is rewritten in place with its stream-scoped consume topic, produce topic and consumer group.
  • Compose generation — a per-stream compose file is emitted, referencing the copied folders and the prebuilt processor images.

All three write into one directory named for the stream. Deleting a match is the mirror image: stop the stack, clean its Kafka topics and cache keys, take the compose down with its volumes, remove the network, then delete the directory.

The interlaced frame-rate doubling

My favourite piece of accumulated knowledge in this codebase, because it looks exactly like a bug.

The operator enters the source frame rate. When the input is flagged interlaced, the generated config gets double what they typed. That is deliberate. The receiver's default deinterlacing mode emits a frame per field, so a 25fps interlaced feed genuinely arrives downstream at 50fps — and the delivery service's health monitor kills its container when throughput falls below three-quarters of the configured rate. Passing the operator's 25 through unchanged would make every interlaced stream restart-loop forever.

Two numbers in two different services that must be changed together, with the reason living in a comment. It's the kind of coupling that only survives if it's written down.

Handling a secret you have to keep

Encrypted inputs take a passphrase, and it needs a specific set of behaviours:

  • Assembled into the connection string in one place, shared by both connection modes so they cannot drift, and emitting nothing at all when encryption is off — the unencrypted address had to stay byte-identical to what it was before the feature existed.
  • Stripped on the way out, not on the way in. The sanitiser sits at the read-response boundary rather than in the data layer, because the update path re-reads the stored record to merge changes — sanitising deeper would silently wipe the stored passphrase on every edit.
  • A blank passphrase on update means keep the existing one, not clear it.
  • Validation errors never echo the submitted value, and log lines on that path redact it.

Stack

Node and TypeScript on the backend, layered routes → controllers → services → repositories over a relational store, with the stream service as the orchestrator. React with Redux Toolkit on the front, plus a socket connection for stats and logs. The generated pipelines are Python services from the streaming project, which this console configures but does not contain.

What I would change

  • The stream service and its controller have grown into thousand-line god objects; new logic belongs in the focused generator classes beside them, and the existing bulk should follow.
  • There is no schema migration story — the ORM only syncs when the tables are missing, so adding a column does nothing to a live database until someone alters it by hand.
  • Endpoint paths are declared in three places, one of which is a partial duplicate. One should be canonical.
  • Two UI kits are installed and both are used depending on the file. Pick one.
  • Credentials are committed in plaintext across compose files and service configs; they belong in injected secrets, and the committed ones should be treated as burned.
  • There are no tests of any kind — the only automated checks are the type checker and the frontend linter.

SDE.name: DFB Analytics Dashboard Automation
SDE.description: A web automation project to scrape and analyze football match data from the DFB analytics dashboard, providing insights and visualizations.

SDE.name: Recon+ Framework
SDE.description: A metadata-driven data reconciliation framework: the datasets to compare, the key columns, and the checks to run are rows in a database, not code. Airflow builds the task graph from those rows and Spark runs the comparison.
highlights: Built a metadata-driven reconciliation framework where the pipeline is configuration rather than code: an Airflow DAG reads a 13-table metamodel and expands its own task graph, so onboarding a dataset is an insert rather than a deployment.

Designed the extension seams — an abstract check interface, an engine-agnostic dataframe wrapper, a connection factory and a pluggable execution-engine registry — so a new data-quality check is one class and a new storage backend is one adapter.

Shipped Spark jobs through Livy with the framework and its entire Python environment staged in object storage, keeping the cluster unmodified and making a framework release a zip upload rather than an image rebuild.
Separated a failing check from a failing job: mismatches and misconfigurations are reported as FAILED and SKIPPED results, so a partial run still publishes every table it did reconcile.

Wrote the reporting layer to two Elasticsearch indices — a summary per check and row-level detail only on failure — bounding write volume on clean runs while keeping failures fully diagnosable in Kibana.
SDE.overview:
Two systems hold what is supposed to be the same data, and somebody has to prove it. A feed lands from an upstream system; it gets loaded into a warehouse table. Recon+ is the thing that checks the two actually agree — and, when they don't, says which rows, which columns, and by how much.

The part that makes it a framework rather than a script is that the pipeline isn't written in code. Which datasets to compare, which columns form the key, which checks to run against which table, where the credentials live — all of it is rows in a database. Onboarding a new dataset is an insert, not a deployment. The Airflow DAG contains no table names at all; it reads them.

  • 6 built-in checks — duplicate keys, field-level value mismatches, row-count drift, missing mandatory fields, data-type mismatches, value-range validation
  • 13 metamodel tables holding clients, pipelines, blocks, tables, column mappings and check assignments
  • Airflow builds the task graph, Spark does the comparison, Elasticsearch and Kibana hold and show the results
  • Written to be extended — a new check is one class implementing one method; a new storage backend is one adapter

Client and dataset names are omitted throughout; the real deployment is configured per client entirely through metamodel rows.
SDE.hld:
The system splits cleanly in two, and the split is the design: Airflow decides what to run by querying a database, and Spark runs it. Neither half knows anything hardcoded about the data.

The DAG is a reader, not a definition

A run is triggered with two values — a client id and a pipeline id. Everything else is discovered. The DAG then does three successive queries, and expands a new set of tasks after each one using Airflow's dynamic task mapping:

  • Blocks — the ordered stages of this client's pipeline
  • Parent notebooks — which orchestrating modules those blocks need, found by joining blocks to tables to check assignments
  • Tables — which datasets each module owns, one mapped task each

Each stage is followed by a flatten-and-dedup step, because the joins legitimately return the same notebook or table more than once and mapping over duplicates would submit the same Spark job twice.

The consequence worth stating plainly: the task graph is a query result. The Airflow UI for a run with forty tables and a run with four looks structurally different, from the same unchanged DAG file. That is the feature, and it is also the debugging cost — you cannot read the DAG file and know what will run.

Why the framework travels through object storage

Spark jobs are submitted over the Livy REST API rather than spark-submit. That choice removes a whole class of coupling: the Airflow workers need only HTTP reach to Livy, not SSH keys for the cluster or a shared filesystem with it.

But it raises the obvious question of how the cluster gets the framework code. The answer is that it doesn't have it installed. Each submission points Livy at three artefacts in object storage: a small entrypoint script, the framework packaged as a zip on the Python path, and the entire Python environment as an archive, unpacked per job and pointed at with spark.pyspark.python.

So the cluster stays vanilla. Deploying a change to a check is re-uploading a zip — no cluster mutation, no image rebuild, and two clients can run different framework versions against the same cluster because the version is a path, not an installation.

The metamodel is read from inside Spark too

This is the part I would flag first in a design review. The Spark job does not receive a self-contained plan. It receives a table name and a config blob, and then calls back to the metamodel itself to fetch its column mappings, its key columns and its check list.

The upside is real: the DAG doesn't have to serialise a whole schema through Airflow's inter-task storage, and a mapping correction takes effect on the next run without redeploying anything. The cost is equally real — every concurrent Spark job is a concurrent client of one MariaDB instance. Table count scales the connection count, and that database is a synchronous dependency of work that is otherwise fully parallel. It is the first thing that would need to change to run this at ten times the width.

Concurrency: sequential where order matters, parallel where it doesn't

Blocks are ordered; tables are not. Blocks exist precisely to express "this group must finish before that one" — a warehouse layer can't be reconciled before the layer feeding it has been. So the block-resolution task is pinned to one instance at a time per run, while the table tasks fan out freely.

Inside a single Spark job there is a third level: the checks for one table run concurrently in a thread pool, sized from the client's own configured concurrency limit. Threads are appropriate here specifically because they aren't doing the work — each one submits Spark operations and waits.

Failure behaviour

The framework draws a hard line between a check that fails and a job that fails, and it matters more than it sounds.

A check finding a mismatch is a result: it returns a status of FAILED with its evidence, gets written to the report, and the pipeline carries on. A check that cannot run at all — no key columns configured, target dataset never loaded — returns SKIPPED rather than throwing, so a misconfiguration shows up as a visibly skipped check instead of a red Airflow task with a stack trace. Only infrastructure failure (metamodel unreachable, dataset missing, Livy session dead) raises.

Two more deliberate choices sit around that:

  • The terminal aggregation task runs on all_done, not on success. A run where three tables out of forty failed still completes and still reports the thirty-seven — a partial result is the normal case in reconciliation, not an exception.
  • Connections are closed in a finally block through the factory that owns them, so a job that dies mid-comparison doesn't leave the metamodel holding sockets. With every executor talking to one database, leaked connections would be the failure that takes down the next run rather than this one.

Results: two indices, and one of them is bounded

Every check emits a summary document — table, check, status, counts, timestamp, run id. Only failures additionally emit detail documents carrying the offending key values and the mismatched source and target values.

That asymmetry is the whole write-volume story. A clean run costs one small document per check regardless of dataset size; the expensive, unbounded output only exists where there is something to look at. Both indices carry the same derived join key, so a dashboard can move from "this check failed" to "here are the rows" without a foreign key.

Where it is designed to be extended

Four seams, in descending order of how well they hold up:

  • A new check — one class, one method, discovered by name from a metamodel row. This works; the six built-ins are all it knows about, and client logic drops in beside them.
  • A new storage backend — one adapter behind a common connection interface. Three exist (relational metamodel, object store, search index).
  • A new search-index version — version-specific adapters chosen at runtime from a config string, because the client library changed incompatibly across three major versions and the deployment target isn't always the same one.
  • A new compute engine — an abstract engine interface plus a factory registry. This is the seam that is declared more than it is built: four engines are named in the enum, one is implemented, and the other three raise. The abstraction is honest about its shape and dishonest about its coverage.
SDE.lld:
The check contract

A check implements exactly one method: it receives a dict holding config, a source dataset and a target dataset, and returns a dict. The return must carry the check's name, its id, and a status of PASSED, FAILED or SKIPPED. There is no second required method — an optional hook lets a check declare extra datasets it wants the parent to pre-fetch, and none of the built-ins use it yet.

Keeping the contract that small is what makes the framework's core promise true: a client writes a check without knowing anything about Airflow, Livy, the metamodel or the reporting layer.

Making checks engine-agnostic — and the escape hatch

Checks never receive a raw Spark DataFrame. They receive a wrapper exposing 15 members — count, filter, select, join, subtract, distinct, dedup, limit, collect, sample, cache, columns, dtypes, plus two purpose-built ones. The stated goal is that a check written today keeps working when the engine underneath changes.

The wrapper is not complete, and rather than pretend otherwise the codebase documents a single sanctioned way through it:

  • raw_df = df.df if hasattr(df, "df") else df

The duplicate-key check uses it, because grouping with Spark column expressions has no equivalent on the interface. I would rather have that one visible, greppable, documented line than an interface that quietly grows a Spark-shaped method every time someone needs one. But it is a debt, not a pattern: every use of it is a place the engine abstraction is a claim rather than a fact.

Two of the fifteen members exist for reasons worth spelling out:

  • Key sanitising replaces nulls and blank strings in key columns with a placeholder before any join. Without it, SQL null semantics silently drop exactly the rows most likely to be broken — a null key joins to nothing, so a reconciliation would report those rows as absent rather than as malformed.
  • Duplicate counting is on the interface rather than composed by callers, because group-count-filter is the single most repeated shape across the checks.

How one table is reconciled

Inside the Spark job, one module handles source-versus-target comparison and a second handles target-only validation. The source-versus-target one runs five phases:

  • Read configuration — the source/target mapping, the column-level mapping including which columns form the key, and the list of checks assigned to this table with their per-assignment parameters.
  • Load source — via a two-value feed type: a flat file in object storage, or a query against a relational source. An unrecognised value logs a warning and defaults to the relational path rather than failing.
  • Load target — from its own configured store.
  • Run the checks — concurrently.
  • Bulk-write the reports — once, for all checks together.

Both datasets are cached before dispatch. This is the detail that makes the thread pool worth having: six checks against one table share one materialisation of the data instead of re-reading it six times. Without the cache, concurrency would multiply the I/O it was meant to hide.

Check discovery, and why I'd change it

A metamodel row names a module. The parent imports it, walks its members, and takes the first class it finds that implements the check interface.

It works, and it means adding a check requires no registration step. It is also implicit in a way I don't like: put two check classes in one module and which one runs depends on member ordering, not on anything anyone wrote down. An explicit registry — a decorator, or a class name in the metamodel row — costs one line per check and removes the ambiguity entirely.

Connections and credentials

Connections come from a factory keyed on type + host + port + database and cached at class level, so the metamodel connection is opened once per job even though four separate phases ask for it. The whole cache is drained in a finally.

Credentials are never in the metamodel. The rows hold a secret ARN, resolved to a credentials dict at runtime, with three resolution paths in priority order: direct credentials passed in, an environment-backed sentinel for the metamodel itself, and ARN lookup for everything else. A single environment flag swaps ARN resolution for a local mock file, which is what makes the framework runnable on a laptop against Docker services with no cloud account.

Joining a result to its evidence

Summary and detail documents land in two different indices and need to be correlated in a dashboard. Each carries a join key: the SHA-256 of run_id : table_id : check_id : time, truncated to 8 bytes and base64url-encoded.

Hashing rather than concatenating keeps the key a fixed short width in every document and every dashboard filter. Truncating to 8 bytes is the questionable half — it is a deliberate size-over-safety trade with a real, if small, collision surface, and the un-truncated version it replaced is still sitting commented out above it. If two documents ever collide, a dashboard silently shows one check's rows under another's summary, which is precisely the kind of wrong that a reconciliation tool cannot afford. It should be wider.

What I would change

  • The metamodel queries are f-string interpolated, including values that arrive in the DAG run configuration. The caller is internal today, which is exactly the argument that stops being true later. These should be parameterised.
  • Nothing measures itself. The report has a duration field; no check populates it, so every document reports zero. The framework can tell you the data is wrong but not how long it took to find out — which is why this write-up carries no throughput figure.
  • The engine enum overpromises. Four engines declared, one implemented, three raising at run time. Either build them or shrink the enum to what exists.
  • One retry, no classification. A dead Livy session and a genuinely unreachable source get the same single retry. Those deserve different treatment: one is worth retrying immediately, the other never is.
  • Schema changes are hand-run SQL files. The metamodel is the whole product's configuration surface and it has no migration tooling — a new environment is a manual seed.
  • The join key should be wider than 8 bytes, per above.

SDE.name: GDELT Event Monitoring
SDE.description: An Airflow pipeline that pulls GDELT's 15-minute global event export, scores conflict events into geographic risk hotspots, and indexes them for a Kibana heatmap. Engine- and sink-agnostic by design — pandas or Spark, Elasticsearch or Postgres, chosen by environment variable — though only one of those four paths runs from a clean checkout.
highlights: Built an engine- and sink-agnostic ingestion pipeline for GDELT's 15-minute global event export: an Airflow DAG fetches and unzips the current release, and a pair of factories selects pandas or Spark and Elasticsearch or Postgres from two environment variables, giving four declared paths through one injected interface.

Mapped GDELT 2.0’s 61-column positional export correctly in both engines — a full Spark StructType and a positional rename in pandas — filtering CAMEO root codes 14 (protest) and 19 (fight) and scoring each location by mention-weighted Goldstein scale to produce geographic hotspots.
Containerised the stack on one compose network: Airflow 2.8.1 with Spark 3.5 and the Elasticsearch-Spark connector baked into the image, plus a Spark master and worker, Elasticsearch 8.12 and Kibana.

Reviewing it since: the raw directory is never cleaned, so neither engine processes the latest batch — Spark re-aggregates all accumulated history each run while pandas reads only glob()[0], one arbitrary file — and the 15-minute document id comes from the wall clock rather than the data, so Kibana shows a cumulative total wearing a per-interval label.

And the architectural lesson: the abstraction is real but sits on the axis nobody varies. Compute engine and database are pluggable; the risk definition, the scoring formula and the aggregation window are hardcoded in duplicate inside both engines, which is where they have already drifted.
SDE.overview:
GDELT publishes a machine-readable record of the world's news every fifteen minutes. This pipeline takes that feed, keeps the events that look like physical conflict, scores each place by how much of it is happening there, and writes the result somewhere a map can read.

Concretely: an Airflow DAG fetches GDELT's lastupdate.txt, downloads the current 15-minute event export and unzips it. A processor then keeps CAMEO root codes 14 (protest) and 19 (fight), weights each event's Goldstein stability score by its mention count, sums that per location, and writes one document per hotspot into Elasticsearch for a Kibana heatmap.

The build was about the architecture, so that is what should be judged. The compute engine and the destination database are both pluggable — two abstract base classes, a factory each, two environment variables. Set EXECUTION_ENGINE to pandas or spark and TARGET_DATABASE to elasticsearch or postgres and you get one of four paths through the same interface. That seam is real in a way this kind of code often isn't: the base classes are enforced, both engines genuinely implement the same transformation, and the sink is injected into the engine rather than imported by it. The 61-column positional schema is also correct in both engines, which is the part of GDELT work that is tedious and easy to get silently wrong.

Two things I would say about it now that I would not have said while writing it.

The seam is on the axis nobody varies. Which dataframe library and which database are decisions you make once, at the start. What changes weekly on a project like this is the question being asked — which event codes count as risk, how threat is scored, what window you aggregate over. None of that is pluggable. All of it is hardcoded, twice, once per engine. So the only logic carrying any judgement is the one thing the design left to be kept in sync by hand, and it has already drifted: the two engines do not read the same data.

And the batch is not a batch. Downloaded files accumulate in the raw directory and nothing deletes them. Spark reads the whole glob, so every run re-aggregates all of history. Pandas reads glob()[0] — one arbitrary file, which after the first run need not be the newest. The 15-minute timestamp stamped on the output comes from the wall clock rather than from the data. What reaches Kibana is a running cumulative total wearing a per-interval label: a chart that climbs for reasons that have nothing to do with the world getting more dangerous.

The honest verdict: I built the abstraction I knew how to build rather than the one the problem needed. Factories and base classes across engine and sink are a recognisable pattern, and executing it cleanly felt like architecture. But an abstraction is only worth what it lets you change cheaply, and I never asked which changes were actually coming. They were all analytical, and they landed in the one place the design left un-abstracted.

The correctness bugs turn out to share a root with that, which is the part I find most useful: nothing in the design names the unit of work. There is no object for "the batch" — no identifier derived from the data, no statement of which interval a run covers, no contract for what happens to a file once it has been consumed. Airflow hands you data_interval_start for exactly this purpose, and the DAG ignores it in favour of whatever is newest right now.

The two layers below take that apart: the architecture layer on what the seams promise and where the guarantees actually live, the implementation layer on the transformation, the document key, and what a clean docker compose up does and does not give you.

Source
SDE.hld:
Four moving parts: a downloader, a processor chosen at runtime, a sink chosen at runtime, and a dashboard reading whatever the sink holds. The design questions worth asking are all about the seams — what each one promises, and whether the promise is the pipeline's or somebody else's.

The two-axis factory, and what it buys

Two abstract base classes carry the design. RiskDataProcessor declares a single method, process_and_write(input_path, sink). DataSink declares what a destination must implement. Each has a factory that maps a string to a class and raises on an unknown value. main.py reads two environment variables, asks each factory for an object, and injects the sink into the processor.

This is worth crediting before criticising, because the failure mode it avoids is common: the seam is not a directory layout that merely looks pluggable. The base classes are abstract and enforced, the dependency runs the right way — the engine receives a sink and knows nothing about which one — and adding a third engine really is a matter of writing one class and adding one line, exactly as the FlinkProcessor would go here comment claims.

What it buys, though, is a choice you make once. And it costs the thing that matters.

The abstraction is Cartesian, not orthogonal

Look at what DataSink actually requires: write_pandas(df) and write_spark(df). Two methods, one per engine. Its docstring calls it "the contract every target database must follow", but the contract is really every database must know about every engine.

So the two axes are not independent. Adding Flink does not mean writing one class — it means writing one class and adding write_flink to every sink that exists. Adding a sink means implementing one method per engine. The design presents itself as N + M and behaves as N × M, and the interface is where that coupling is written down rather than hidden.

There are cleaner shapes. A single write(df) per sink, with the engine responsible for handing over a representation the sink understands. Or dispatch inside the sink on the type it receives. Or — most honest at real scale — drop the pretence of one interface and register writers explicitly per (engine, sink) pair, so the N × M cost is visible in the code rather than discovered when you add the third engine.

The business logic is duplicated, and has drifted

Both engines implement the same forty lines of analysis: filter to two CAMEO root codes, drop rows without coordinates, compute NumMentions × −GoldsteinScale, group by location, sum, and build a document id. One in pandas, one in Spark DSL.

Two implementations of one rule is two places for it to drift, and it has:

  • Spark reads the whole input glob. Pandas reads glob()[0] — a single file, chosen by whatever order the filesystem returns. Same environment variable, same "pipeline", a different quantity of data.
  • Both take first(SOURCEURL) per group. In pandas that is deterministic by row order; in Spark, first without an ordering is not. The sample link attached to a hotspot differs between engines and between Spark runs.

This is the part I would raise first in a design review of my own work. The things a risk pipeline is asked to change are analytical: add root code 18 for assault, weight recent mentions more heavily, aggregate over 24 hours instead of whatever happens to be on disk. Every one of those is a two-file edit that no test covers, in the only code here with any judgement in it. Meanwhile the engine choice — the thing the architecture is built around — has been exercised approximately twice.

Where the guarantee lives

Both engines carry a comment reading THE IDEMPOTENCY & TIME-SERIES FIX, and behind it a document id built from the location name and the 15-minute bucket. Re-run the same batch and you should overwrite rather than duplicate.

That holds for Elasticsearch, which is handed the id as _id and upserts on it. It does not hold for Postgres, which appends with no key and no conflict clause — the pandas path via to_sql(if_exists='append'), the Spark path via mode('append'). Re-run against Postgres and every row duplicates.

So a guarantee advertised as a property of the pipeline is really a property of one sink. And the reason it can go unnoticed is structural: DataSink has nowhere for a sink to declare whether it can upsert. The interface only says "write". A pipeline whose correctness depends on a capability its own abstraction cannot express has put the boundary in the wrong place — either the sink contract should require upsert semantics and Postgres should implement them, or the pipeline should stop claiming idempotency it cannot enforce.

The unit of work is missing

This is the root the correctness problems grow from. Nothing in the system represents "the batch being processed".

  • The DAG downloads whatever lastupdate.txt currently points at, so a run is not tied to an interval. catchup=False and a 15-minute schedule make that explicit — there is no backfill, because a run has no data interval to backfill.
  • The output timestamp and document id come from datetime.utcnow() at execution time, not from the data. With retries=2, a retry one minute later can download a different file and stamp it into a different bucket, so the retry is neither a no-op nor a correction.
  • Nothing deletes a consumed file, so the input to any given run is "every file ever downloaded".

Airflow already models this. data_interval_start gives each run an identity derived from the schedule rather than the clock; GDELT's own filenames and DATEADDED column give each batch an identity derived from the data. Keying on either would make the run idempotent, the retries safe and the series meaningful. Using utcnow() instead makes the id look data-derived while behaving like a timestamp of when the job happened to run.

Engine selection happens at parse time

The DAG chooses its engine with a top-level Variable.get("active_execution_engine") and then builds either a SparkSubmitOperator or a BashOperator in an if. Two consequences:

  • It queries the metadata database on every DAG parse, which the scheduler does continuously — the standard Airflow anti-pattern for top-level code.
  • Flipping the variable rewrites the DAG's topology, because the two branches have different task_ids. History for the task that no longer exists is orphaned rather than continued.

The shape that does what was intended is one task whose behaviour is parameterised, or a branch operator that keeps both tasks in the graph — leaving the graph stable and the choice per-run rather than global.

What a clean checkout actually runs

Four declared paths. From docker compose up on a fresh clone, one of them works:

  • Both Postgres paths are dead. The sink connects as user admin to database risk_db. The compose file provisions Postgres as airflow/airflow with database airflow, for Airflow's own metadata. Neither the user nor the database is ever created.
  • The Spark path needs manual setup. SparkSubmitOperator uses conn_id='spark_default', and nothing in the compose file or image provisions that connection — nor the active_execution_engine variable that selects the branch. Both have to be entered in the Airflow UI by hand, and neither is recorded anywhere in the repository.

That leaves pandas → Elasticsearch, the default on both variables. The architecture is not wrong about being extensible; it is untested at three of its four corners, and the compose file quietly disagrees with the code about what exists. Provisioning the connection and the variable as environment variables, and creating risk_db in an init script, is a small amount of work that would turn a claim into a demonstrable fact.
SDE.lld:
The transformation

GDELT 2.0's event export is 61 tab-separated columns with no header, so everything starts with getting positions right. Both engines do, which is worth stating plainly because it is the easiest thing here to get silently wrong — an off-by-one in the column map produces plausible numbers from the wrong field.

  • Spark declares a StructType covering all 61 fields, naming the ten it cares about and padding the rest as _c5–_c24 (the two actor blocks) and _c35–_c50 (the two actor-geography blocks). The arithmetic checks out: 5 + 20 + 10 + 16 + 10 = 61.
  • Pandas reads headerless and renames seven integer positions — 28, 30, 31, 52, 56, 57, 60. Each matches the codebook.

The analysis is then four steps: keep EventRootCode in {14, 19}; drop rows with no action coordinates; compute Threat_Level = NumMentions × (GoldsteinScale × −1); group by (name, lat, long) and sum, counting incidents and taking one sample source URL.

What the threat score measures

Worth being exact, because the field is called Total_Threat_Score and that name claims more than the formula delivers.

Goldstein assigns each CAMEO event type a stability impact from −10 to +10. Root codes 14 and 19 are negative, so negating gives a positive magnitude — the sign convention is sound for the codes selected. But multiplying by NumMentions means the score is the amount of press an event received, weighted by how bad that type of event is. A single heavily covered protest outranks many uncovered ones. What the map ranks is media attention to conflict, which correlates with conflict and is not the same thing — and coverage is unevenly distributed by language, region and news infrastructure in ways that bias the output systematically, not randomly.

Two smaller consequences of the same formula: because nothing clamps the sign, an event in these root codes with a positive Goldstein value would subtract from its location's total and mask a hotspot; and because there is no normalisation, the score has no unit and is comparable only against itself. Calling the field a score rather than an index is the part I would change first — naming it for what it is would have kept me honest about it.

The scope is also narrower than "risk" implies: 2 of GDELT's 20 CAMEO root codes. Assault (18), coercion (17), threats (13) and mass violence (20) are all excluded. That is a defensible starting filter, but it is a choice the code makes silently and the dashboard label does not mention.

The document key loses rows

Both engines group by (ActionGeo_FullName, ActionGeo_Lat, ActionGeo_Long) and then build the Elasticsearch document id from the name and the timestamp only, spaces stripped.

The grouping key and the document key therefore disagree. Two distinct coordinate pairs sharing a FullName — which GDELT produces routinely, since names repeat across regions and resolve at different geographic precisions — become two aggregated rows carrying the same doc_id. Elasticsearch treats the second as an update of the first and the earlier row is gone, silently, with no error and no count mismatch to notice. Postgres keeps both, so the two sinks disagree about how many hotspots exist.

The fix is to key on what was grouped on. It also wants a real delimiter: stripping spaces from a name and joining with an underscore is not injective, so distinct names can collide into one id.

Time handling

Both engines round the current time down to a 15-minute boundary and use it for the ISO timestamp and for the id suffix:

  • The value comes from datetime.utcnow(), which returns a naive datetime — so .isoformat() emits a timestamp with no offset, and the reader decides what zone it meant. It is also deprecated from Python 3.12 in favour of datetime.now(timezone.utc), which would produce an unambiguous value as a side effect of being current.
  • In the Spark path the rounding happens on the driver and is broadcast as a literal, which is correct — a per-row current_timestamp() would have split one batch across two buckets.
  • The bucket describes when the job ran, not which data it read. On a retry a minute later the boundary may differ, and the same events land under a second id.

The accumulating raw directory

This is the defect with the largest effect on what a viewer of the dashboard would conclude, and it is an interaction rather than a single mistake.

The DAG extracts each download into /opt/airflow/dags/data/raw and nothing ever removes a file. The processors read *.CSV from that directory. So on run n:

  • Spark reads all n files and re-aggregates the entire accumulated history, then writes it under a document id stamped with the current 15-minute bucket. Every run produces a fresh snapshot of a cumulative total, so the Kibana time series rises monotonically by construction — it is a running sum presented as a per-interval reading. A rising line means the pipeline has been up for longer, not that risk has increased.
  • Pandas reads glob.glob(input_path)[0]. One file. glob does not sort, so after the first run the file processed need not be — and generally will not be — the one just downloaded. The result is the same numbers re-stamped with a new timestamp every fifteen minutes: a flat line that looks like a stable world.

Both engines are wrong, in opposite directions, and neither fails. The download task succeeds, the processing task succeeds, the dashboard populates. Nothing in the pipeline compares what it read against what it was supposed to read, which is the general lesson — a batch pipeline needs to assert its input, not just glob it.

Smaller things I would fix

  • No timeout on either HTTP call. Both requests.get calls omit timeout, so a hung GDELT endpoint blocks the worker slot indefinitely — three times over, given retries=2.
  • Credentials and hosts are hardcoded in the sinks — admin:admin in the Postgres URL and JDBC options, http://elasticsearch:9200 in the Elastic sink. So the sink is pluggable in which kind of database but not which instance; pointing it at anything real means editing source. These belong in environment variables or an Airflow connection.
  • The dependency install is unpinned: pip install ... pandas elasticsearch against a compose file pinned to Elasticsearch 8.12.0. The Python client has since gone to 9.x, and a major-version mismatch against an 8.x cluster is rejected, so rebuilding the image today breaks the sink that used to work. Pinning the client to the server line is the fix; a requirements.txt with versions is the habit.
  • The _source filter is a no-op. The Elastic sink strips a key called _id while building each document, but the column is named doc_id — so nothing is stripped and the id is stored in the document as well as being the document's id.
  • self.spark.stop() inside process_and_write tears down a session obtained with getOrCreate(), which the processor may not have created. It also makes the processor single-use, which quietly contradicts the base class reading like a reusable component.
  • Two Spark installations. Spark 3.5 is baked into the Airflow image and run as separate master and worker services, so which one executes a submit depends on a connection that is never provisioned.
  • Error reporting loses the traceback. main.py catches everything and prints str(e), so a Spark failure arrives as one line without the stack that would explain it.
  • The Spark images are pinned to the bitnamilegacy namespace, a mirror kept for compatibility rather than maintained — fine for a prototype, not something to build on.

The four use cases, and the one that got built

The repository carries design notes for four applications of the same feed — supply-chain risk, commodity price anxiety, brand-reputation contagion, and ESG compliance — each naming the GDELT fields it would need. They are proposals rather than specifications, and they still carry the citation markers of the tool that drafted them against the GDELT codebook; they should be either cleaned up or marked clearly as sketches.

Only the first is implemented, and it differs from its own note in a way worth recording: the note specifies aggregation over a rolling 24-hour window, and the code has no window at all — it aggregates whatever files are on disk. That is the same gap I found writing up an earlier project, arriving from the other direction. There, a design document claimed structure the code did not have. Here, a design note specified a windowing rule and the code silently declined it, which is how the cumulative-total bug got to look like a feature.

What I would change, in order

  • Give the batch an identity. Derive the interval from Airflow's data_interval_start or from GDELT's own filename, key the document on it, and process exactly the files belonging to it.
  • Consume the input. Move or delete a file once processed, and fail loudly if the expected file for an interval is absent, rather than quietly globbing whatever remains.
  • Collapse the duplicated analysis. One declarative description of the filter, the score and the grouping, with the engines reduced to executing it — so there is one place to change what "risk" means.
  • Fix the document key to match the grouping key, with a delimiter that cannot collide.
  • Decide where idempotency lives. Either require upsert in the sink contract and implement ON CONFLICT for Postgres, or stop describing the pipeline as idempotent.
  • Make the four paths real — provision the Spark connection and the engine variable in the compose file, create risk_db, and run all four combinations once — or delete the ones that are not going to be supported.
  • Externalise hosts and credentials, pin the dependencies, and add timeouts to the HTTP calls.
  • Rename the score to say what it measures, and record the media-attention bias next to the dashboard rather than only in a write-up.
  • Measure a run. Nothing here has a recorded event count or runtime, so the pandas-versus-Spark choice the whole architecture exists to offer has never been informed by a number.

SDE.name: ccwc
SDE.description: A from-scratch reimplementation of Unix wc in 119 lines of C++ — lines, words, bytes and UTF-8 characters derived in a single pass over 64 KiB blocks, from a file or from stdin. The scan is careful: word state survives a block boundary and codepoints are counted with no locale. The reporting then discards most of what it counted, and -m is unreachable in all sixteen ways you can call it.
highlights: Reimplemented Unix wc from scratch in C++ in 119 lines, deriving line, word, byte and UTF-8 character counts in a single traversal of 64 KiB blocks — constant memory regardless of input size, and no allocation after startup.
Counted UTF-8 codepoints with no locale, no wide-character conversion and no allocation, by testing each byte against the continuation-byte bit pattern rather than decoding text.
Held word-boundary state outside the read loop so a word split across a 64 KiB block boundary is counted once — the silent over-count that a test file smaller than one block can never expose.
Shared one scanning routine between a file and standard input by taking a std::istream reference, so there is no second read loop to keep in sync and no source check inside the hot loop.

Reviewing it since: traced all sixteen flag combinations through the reporting logic and found only five report everything asked for — the defaults guard omits the character flag, which makes the -m branch dead code in every possible invocation. The repository already held a 342 KB fixture and the reference binary; one differential test against wc would have caught all eleven cases in under a minute.

metrics.label: -m honoured
metrics.source: Defaults guard omits it; branch is dead

SDE.overview:
How big is this file? That is the question wc answers, on every Unix machine, and has since 1971 — how many lines, how many words, how many bytes. This is that program, rebuilt from scratch in C++ rather than read about: 119 lines in one file, three commits, all on the same day, no dependencies beyond the standard library.

It handles -l lines, -w words, -c bytes and -m characters, reads either a named file or standard input, and with no flags reports all three of the defaults at once. The exercise it follows names the binary ccwc and supplies a Project Gutenberg copy of The Art of War as the test file, which is what both of those are doing in the repository.

The interesting decision is that it never holds the file. The naive version of this program reads lines into a string and counts them, which means memory grows with the largest line and the file is walked once per thing you asked for. This one reads the input in fixed 64 KiB blocks into a single stack buffer and derives all four counts in one traversal of each block. Memory is constant regardless of whether the input is a kilobyte or a hundred gigabytes, and the byte count, the line count, the word count and the character count all fall out of the same loop.

Two details in that loop are the reason it was worth writing rather than reading about. A word can be split by a block boundary — read 64 KiB and you may well stop in the middle of one — and the flag tracking whether the scanner is currently inside a word is declared outside the read loop specifically so it survives into the next block. Get that wrong and every 64 KiB adds a phantom word. And characters are not bytes: a UTF-8 codepoint is one to four bytes, and the loop separates the two by skipping continuation bytes — any byte whose top two bits are 10 — which counts codepoints with no locale, no wide-character conversion and no allocation at all.

Then it decides what to print, and that is where it comes apart. The four flags are collected into four independent booleans, which is right, and then reported through a single if/else chain that can emit at most one of them. Ask for lines and words together and you get lines. And there is a worse case: a guard that fills in the defaults when no flag was given omits the character flag from its test, so an invocation that asked only for -m is treated as though it asked for nothing, and the branch that prints characters sits behind a condition that guard has just made impossible to satisfy. Push all sixteen possible flag combinations through it and five report everything that was asked for; eleven silently report less; and -m, in all eight combinations that contain it, is never honoured once.

The honest verdict is not about the bug, it is about the test file. The repository contains a 342,190-byte fixture. The reference implementation was installed on the same machine. One shell loop diffing this program's output against wc's across the flag set would have found all of this in under a minute, and it was never run — the program was checked by looking at it, on the inputs it was expected to handle. I got the hard half right, the part about buffers and boundaries and encodings, and shipped the easy half broken, because I verified the half I found interesting.

The two layers below take it apart: the architecture layer on what the program guarantees and how it behaves at the edges, the implementation layer on the exact per-byte contracts, the sixteen-combination trace, and a 54 KiB ARM64 executable that is checked into the repository.

Source
SDE.hld:
Four stages, one buffer, no allocation after startup. At this size the architecture is legible in a single reading, which makes it a good place to be precise about the three things that actually matter in a counting tool: what it guarantees, what it does at the boundaries, and what it does when you ask it something it cannot answer.

The shape

  • Argument scan. A single pass over argv setting four independent booleans, with anything unrecognised treated as the input path.
  • Stream selection. One std::istream* pointing at either std::cin or an ifstream opened in ios::binary.
  • The scan. process_stream(std::istream&, ...) reads 64 KiB at a time and accumulates four counters by reference.
  • The dispatch. A default-fill guard, then an if/else chain that prints.

The stream selection deserves the credit it looks too small to deserve. Because the scanner takes an istream& rather than a filename, reading a file and reading a pipe are the same code path — there is no second loop to keep in sync, and no branch inside the hot loop asking where the bytes came from. That is the whole of the abstraction, and it is the correct amount of it for a program this size.

What it guarantees

  • Constant memory. One 64 KiB buffer, sized at compile time. Nothing scales with the input, so there is no largest-line failure mode and no reason a hundred-gigabyte file behaves differently from a small one.
  • One traversal. All four counts come out of a single walk of each block. Asking for one number costs exactly what asking for four costs.
  • Byte-exactness. The file is opened in binary mode, so no newline translation happens between the disk and the count — a CRLF file reports the bytes it actually contains.
  • No locale dependence in the character count. Codepoints are identified structurally, from the bit pattern of each byte, rather than by asking the C library to decode text according to an environment variable.

The boundary is the whole problem

Chunked counting is easy to write and easy to get subtly wrong, and both of the classic mistakes are avoided here — which is worth stating explicitly, because they are invisible when it works.

State has to outlive the block. Words are counted on entry: the scanner increments when it sees a non-space byte while not already inside a word. That "inside a word" flag lives outside the read loop, so when a block ends mid-word the next block resumes knowing it is mid-word and does not count the remainder as a new one. Move that one declaration inside the loop and the program still compiles, still passes any test whose input is smaller than 64 KiB, and over-reports every large file by roughly one word per block.

The last block is short. The read loop's condition is in.read(buf, N) || in.gcount() > 0. A stream that hits end-of-file part way through a read sets its failure bit and converts to false, so the obvious loop discards the final partial block — everything after the last 64 KiB boundary. The second clause catches exactly that case, and terminates correctly on the following iteration because a failed stream reads nothing and reports a count of zero.

Neither of these has been proven by test — there is no test in the repository — but both are visible in the source, and both are the kind of thing a reviewer should be able to check by reading, which is the argument for keeping the scan this small.

Where the design gives up

The flags go in as four independent bits and come out through a structure that can only express one answer. This is not a typo in one branch; it is a shape mismatch, and it produces three distinct classes of wrong behaviour.

Combinations collapse. The chain tests for all three defaults together, then falls through to bytes, then lines, then words, each in an else if. So -l -w prints lines and drops words without comment, and -c -l prints bytes and drops lines. The program has the number. It computed it in the same loop. It just has nowhere to say it.

One flag is unreachable. The default-fill guard sets bytes, lines and words when all three are unset — and does not consider the character flag when deciding whether anything was asked for. So ccwc -m file walks into that guard with all three false, walks out with all three true, and lands in the first branch printing bytes, lines and words. Meanwhile the branch that prints characters requires all three to be false, which the guard has just guaranteed they are not. It is dead code in every possible invocation, and the implementation layer traces all sixteen combinations to show there is no exception.

Output shape is inconsistent. The default branch prints one line; the single-flag branches print a newline before the filename, so ccwc -c file emits the number and the filename on two separate lines. Real wc also orders its columns lines, words, bytes, where this prints bytes, lines, words with the words spelled out as labels. Nothing here is wrong in isolation — it is simply not a drop-in replacement, which for a clone is the only interesting property.

How it behaves when you hold it wrong

Failure behaviour is where a small tool reveals whether it was designed or merely finished. Held against the source:

  • A missing file exits 1 with error opening file on stderr. Correct in structure — non-zero status, message on the right stream — and unhelpful in content, because it does not name the file or say why, which is the entire value of the message when it appears inside a script.
  • An unknown flag becomes a filename. The argument scan's final else treats anything unmatched as the path, so ccwc -x file reports a file-open failure for -x. The user is told the wrong thing about the wrong argument.
  • Two files silently become one. Each non-flag argument overwrites the stored path, so ccwc a.txt b.txt counts b.txt and never mentions a.txt. Real wc counts both and prints a total. Silently answering a different question than the one asked is the worst of the failures on this page.
  • The stdin convention is half-implemented. A bare - conventionally means "read standard input". This code prints incorrect argument type to stderr for it, then does not exit — and since no path was recorded, falls through and reads standard input anyway. The behaviour is right by accident and the diagnostic is wrong on purpose.

The shape it should have had

The fix is not a rewrite, it is deleting the chain. Keep the scan exactly as it is — it is the part that is right — and replace the reporting with an ordered emit: decide the requested set once (defaults applied only when the set is genuinely empty, counting all flags including -m), then walk the counters in wc's documented column order and print each one that was requested, space-separated, on one line. That is a loop over four entries instead of five branches, it makes every combination expressible by construction, and it removes the possibility of a flag having no reachable branch.

Beyond that: accumulate paths into a vector rather than a scalar, run the scan per path and print a totals row when there is more than one; reject unrecognised flags instead of reinterpreting them as filenames; treat - as stdin rather than as an error; and include the failing path and strerror in the open-failure message.

And measure it. Nothing on this page is a benchmark. The program has never been timed against wc, which matters because the one-pass 64 KiB design is a performance argument and it is currently unsupported — GNU wc has an ASCII fast path and uses memchr for line counting, so a naive byte-at-a-time loop may well be slower despite the better asymptotics. The throughput slot on this page is empty for exactly that reason, and filling it in is the next thing to do.
SDE.lld:
The four contracts

Every count in the program is one predicate evaluated per byte, inside a single loop over the block. Stated exactly, because the precision is the point:

  • Bytes. Incremented once per block by the stream's reported read count, not once per byte. Unconditional — there is no input for which a byte is read and not counted.
  • Lines. Incremented on '\n'. This counts newlines, not lines, so a final line with no trailing newline is not counted — matching wc, which does the same thing, and worth knowing rather than discovering.
  • Characters. Incremented when (c & 0xC0) != 0x80 — that is, on every byte that is not a UTF-8 continuation byte. Continuation bytes are exactly those beginning 10; ASCII bytes begin 0 and lead bytes begin 11, so both are counted and the two or three bytes trailing a lead byte are not. One increment per codepoint, from bit arithmetic alone.
  • Words. Incremented on the transition from outside a word to inside one: if the byte is whitespace the in-word flag clears, otherwise, if the flag was clear, it sets and the counter advances. Counting entries rather than separators is what makes runs of whitespace, leading whitespace and trailing whitespace all behave correctly without a special case.

Two smaller things in that loop are right in a way that is easy to miss. isspace is called on the byte cast to unsigned char, which is not pedantry: char is signed on x86 and ARM, every byte of a non-ASCII UTF-8 sequence has its top bit set, and passing a negative value to isspace is undefined behaviour. The cast is the difference between this working on UTF-8 input and being allowed to do anything at all. And the program never calls setlocale, so it runs in the "C" locale where isspace is true for exactly six ASCII bytes — which makes word splitting deterministic and independent of the caller's environment.

What the word rule does not do is split on non-ASCII whitespace. A no-break space (U+00A0) or an ideographic space (U+3000) is a multi-byte sequence with no ASCII space in it, so text using them reads as one long word. That is the same behaviour as byte-oriented wc in the C locale, so it is a limitation of the model rather than a defect against it — but the program counts characters as codepoints and words as bytes, and those two decisions are not consistent with each other.

The block boundary, precisely

The scanner's only cross-block state is the in-word flag, and it is the only cross-block state needed: bytes, lines and characters are all decided by the current byte alone, while words are decided by the current byte and whether the previous one was whitespace. Declaring the flag outside the read loop is therefore not a stylistic choice, it is the correctness condition.

Worth being concrete about the cost of getting it wrong, since the failure is silent: with the declaration moved inside the loop, every block boundary that falls inside a word adds one phantom word. On a 342 KiB file that is five extra blocks and up to five extra words out of fifty-eight thousand — a 0.008% error, undetectable by eye, and never triggered at all by a test file smaller than 64 KiB. This is the class of bug that only a differential test against a reference implementation catches, which is the argument for having run one.

All sixteen ways to call it

The reporting logic is a default-fill guard followed by a five-branch chain. The guard:

  • if (!is_count_bytes && !is_count_words && !is_count_lines) then set all three true.

And the chain, in source order: all three together, then bytes, then lines, then words, then characters — each after the first an else if. Pushing every flag subset through both gives the complete behaviour, and the pattern is not subtle once written down:

  • Answered correctly (5): no flags, -c, -l, -w, and -c -l -w. In each of these the requested set happens to be either a single counter or exactly the three defaults, which are the only two things the chain can express.
  • Silently under-reports (11): every other combination. Any pair of defaults collapses to whichever comes first in the chain — -c -l and -c -w print bytes only, -l -w prints lines only. And every one of the eight combinations containing -m drops it.

-m alone is the clearest case. Trace it: the character flag is set, the other three are not. The guard's test asks whether bytes, words and lines are all unset — they are — so it sets all three, having never looked at the character flag. The chain's first branch now matches, and the program prints bytes, lines and words. ccwc -m file and ccwc file produce byte-identical output. The character counter was computed in the loop, correctly, and thrown away.

And the character branch cannot be reached from anywhere else either, because it requires bytes, lines and words all false, and any invocation in which all three are false is precisely the invocation the guard rewrites. The counter that required the only genuinely non-obvious code in the program — the UTF-8 bit test — is the one whose output is unreachable. Five source lines that can never execute.

Output formatting

  • The column order differs from wc. Real wc prints lines, words, bytes in that order, as bare numbers. This prints bytes, lines, words, each followed by a spelled-out label — 342190 bytes 7145 lines 58164 words. Readable, and not parseable by anything expecting wc.
  • The single-flag branches emit a newline too early. Each of them ends with endl, and the filename is printed after the branch, so ccwc -c file produces the count on one line and  file on the next. The default branch does not end with endl and so prints on one line — meaning the layout changes depending on which flags were passed.
  • The default branch double-spaces the filename, since it ends with a trailing space and the filename is prefixed with another one.
  • Reading stdin still prints a leading space in the single-flag branches, because only the filename is conditional, not the separator before it.

Smaller things in the source

  • The buffer is 64 KiB on the stack. Fine on a normal thread, worth knowing rather than assuming: it is 8 MiB of a typical Linux main thread's stack budget away from mattering, but it would be the first thing to move if the scan were ever called on a thread with a small stack.
  • <algorithm> and <system_error> are included and unused. The system_error include in particular suggests an intent to report why a file failed to open, which the error path never does.
  • std::filesystem::path holds the filename and is used only to be assigned a string and converted back to one, so the include buys nothing here — though it is the right type to have reached for if the program grows to check whether the argument is a directory, which it currently does not and will happily attempt to read.
  • using namespace std; at file scope, which at 119 lines costs nothing and is the habit that stops being free at ten times the size.

What is in the repository that should not be

A compiled executable is checked in. The file ccwc in the repository root is not a script — it is a 55,664-byte ELF binary for ARM64, dynamically linked against /system/bin/linker64, which identifies it specifically as an Android build, from a Termux toolchain. It is unstripped. So the repository ships a binary that will not run on any of the machines a reader is likely to have, and no way to produce one that will.

The mechanism is worth naming because it is funnier and more instructive than carelessness.
