The commit that added it is titled "added make file" and contains no Makefile — it adds the binary and renames wc_tool.cpp to main.cpp. The .gitignore, a 69-line C++ template copied in on the first commit, has an Executables section listing *.exe, *.out and *.app, none of which match a file simply called ccwc. Two lines below that, under CMake generated files, it ignores Makefile — so a hand-written Makefile could not have been committed even if one existed. The ignore rules let the build output through and blocked the build instructions.

The fix is one line in .gitignore and a git rm --cached, but the general lesson is the one I would rather state: a template .gitignore describes a project someone else had. Reading the 69 lines once, against what this project actually produces, was cheaper than shipping an unrunnable artifact as the repository's most prominent file.

What is not here

There is no test, and there was never a reason for that. The repository contains test.txt, 342,190 bytes of it, added in the same commit as the source. The reference implementation was installed on the machine that ran the build. The differential test is one line of shell — compare this program's output to wc's for each flag combination on that fixture — and it would have failed immediately on -m, on every pair of default flags, and on the output format. It was never written.

That is the finding I would lead with about my own work here, ahead of any individual bug. The fixture was treated as something to look at output for, rather than something to compare output against, and the gap between those two is the difference between eleven silent defects and none.

What I would change

  • Replace the if/else chain with an ordered emit — a list of (flag, counter, column) walked in wc's order, printing each requested entry — so every combination is expressible by construction and no flag can have an unreachable branch.
  • Include -m in the defaults test, which is the one-token fix, but do it as part of the change above rather than instead of it, since the chain would still collapse pairs.
  • Match wc's output exactly — lines, words, bytes, bare numbers, one line, one space before the filename — and add --help so the differences that remain are deliberate.
  • Take a vector of paths, count each, and print a totals row when there is more than one.
  • Reject unknown flags rather than reinterpreting them as filenames, accept - as stdin, and put the path and strerror(errno) in the open-failure message.
  • Write the differential test against wc over the committed fixture and the full flag set, and add a case larger than 64 KiB with words straddling a block boundary so the in-word invariant is actually covered.
  • Add a Makefile and stop ignoring it, remove the ARM64 binary from history, and decide the ignore rules from what the project builds.
  • Benchmark it against wc before making any claim about the one-pass design, since GNU wc's memchr-based line counting and ASCII fast path may beat a byte-at-a-time loop outright.

SDE.name: BOOTS
SDE.description: A private, self-hosted, voice-first AI assistant: an Android client with a "Hey BOOTS" wake word talks to a FastAPI brain running a local LLM on my own laptop over Tailscale, with a knowledge graph, tool-calling, and on-device fallback when the laptop is unreachable. Built through 45 shipped phases plus a 5-agent adversarial audit that found and fixed 19 concurrency, reliability and performance defects device-verified on real hardware.
highlights: Built a two-node personal AI assistant end to end: a Jetpack Compose Android app (138 Kotlin files, ~12,450 lines) talking to a FastAPI agent brain (4,650 lines of Python) running Ollama/Qwen2.5-7B on my own GPU laptop, connected over Tailscale with bearer-token auth and SQLCipher encryption at rest on both ends.

Implemented a tool-calling agent loop with a deterministic verification backstop after live testing showed the LLM claiming it had stored a reminder or fact without ever calling the tool — a known small-model reliability gap the design anticipated rather than discovered by accident, and a heuristic gate that routes store/recall phrasing to the safe non-streamed path so a streamed chitchat turn can never silently skip a real write.

Ran a structured, read-only 5-agent robustness audit (database, error-detective, performance, SRE, Kotlin-concurrency personas) against my own shipped code, producing 19 severity-ranked findings — then fixed and device-verified 12 of them, including a one-line WebSocket ping-interval fix that resolved a "wake goes silent" bug traced through three compounding root causes (a half-open socket, a fire-and-forget mic release, and a detached async task with no terminal event).

Measured every performance claim on real hardware rather than estimating: forcing full GPU offload lifted backend throughput 25.5→37.3 tok/s (+46%), and a voice-latency capture that traced an 18.6-second turn down to whisper running 5-10x slower than its own documented baseline under real memory pressure — with the exact confound (RAM at 99%) shown in the guardian's own log rather than assumed.

Chose SQLite autocommit plus WAL plus a 5-second busy timeout to eliminate an entire class of silent write loss, after finding a held write transaction across a multi-second LLM call was colliding with background writers that all swallowed their own exceptions — the fix removes the deadlock class rather than patching the one call site that happened to be observed.
SDE.overview:
Say "Hey BOOTS" to any screen on my phone, and a floating voice orb answers — using an LLM running on my own laptop, not a cloud API. The phone is a thin client: wake word, voice capture, a chat UI, local encrypted storage. The laptop is the brain: a FastAPI agent that does tool-calling, retrieval over a personal knowledge graph, web search with fact-checking, and text-to-speech, backed by Ollama running Qwen2.5-7B on an RTX 4050. They talk over Tailscale, so it works from anywhere without a cloud bill or a port-forward. When the laptop is asleep or unreachable, the phone falls back to a small on-device model for capture and local recall — the assistant degrades, it never goes silent.

This is a solo, single-user project, not a product — there is no distribution, no other users, and the repository is private. What I want this write-up to show instead is the engineering discipline behind it, because that's the part that transfers: every phase in PLAN.md's dependency graph is either shipped-and-verified or explicitly logged as not started, every non-obvious fix is written down in a 41-entry gotcha log the moment it's found, and every performance number on this page came from a real request against real hardware — including the negative ones. The on-device GPU delegate, for instance, is recorded as verified-safe but delivering no speedup on this specific phone, because that's what actually happened.

The part I'd point a reviewer at is the audit. After the core system shipped, I ran a read-only review of my own code using five adversarial personas — database, error-detective, performance, SRE, concurrency — each looking for a different failure mode, explicitly told to change nothing. That surfaced 19 findings ranked by severity, including a real production bug already live: users had reported the wake word going "sometimes very late, all fucked up," and the audit traced it to three separate defects compounding — a WebSocket with no ping interval that let a dead connection hang forever, a microphone release that fired without waiting for it to finish, and an error branch that skipped releasing the mic at all. Any one of the three would have been a plausible standalone fix; finding all three at once meant the actual fix held. Twelve of the nineteen findings are now fixed and device-verified; the rest are open, prioritized, and undisguised as done.

The honest limits: the on-device model is Gemma 3 1B, genuinely too small for reliable classification — the design routes almost everything through deterministic heuristics first and only asks the small model for what's left, because trusting it directly produced real observed failures during development. The voice pipeline's dominant latency cost turned out not to be the thing I expected (a fixed silence-detection window) but whisper's raw transcription speed under memory pressure, and I've recorded that as an upper bound pending a re-measurement on a resource-normal machine rather than presenting it as a settled number. And it's a household of one: nothing here has been used by, or designed for, anyone but me.

No public source link — the repository is private, since it touches my own personal data, household setup, and a device on my home network.
SDE.hld:
Two independent processes across two machines, joined by one contract: a bearer-token HTTP/WS API over Tailscale. The interesting design decisions are all about what happens when either side of that link is slow, dead, or lying — because a personal assistant that only works when everything is healthy isn't one you can trust.

Two nodes, one degrading contract

The phone is deliberately dumb by default and gets smarter only when the brain is reachable. A tiny on-device Gemma 3 1B model (fine-tuned for this app's own extraction format) handles capture and local recall when the laptop can't be reached; when it can, every routing decision — is this a statement to store, a question to answer, a reminder to set, something to fact-check — is handed to the 7B model on the laptop, because the small model measurably gets this wrong often enough to be unusable for it (documented directly in the code as a "small-model reality" note, not a hunch).

The degrade path is explicit rather than assumed: laptop up → full tool-calling, RAG, web search; laptop asleep or unreachable → phone captures and answers locally, already-scheduled reminders still fire on-device. Nothing silently stops working; every state is a named, expected mode.

Small-model reliability is treated as a fact to defend against, not a bug to fix

This shows up twice, in two different failure shapes, and both are handled the same way: don't trust a single model output for anything that must actually happen.

The model claims an action it didn't take. agent.py's tool-calling loop had a real observed failure where the LLM replied "I've set a reminder" without ever calling set_reminder — the confirmation was fabricated, the write never happened. The fix is a second, narrower model call: after any no-tool-call turn, ask a forced yes/no question — "did this message need a store/reminder tool?" — and only force a real tool call if the answer is yes. That turns one unreliable judgment into a cheap, separately-verifiable one.

The model derails mid-generation. Qwen2.5 is Chinese-origin and was observed, live, code-switching into Chinese partway through an English reply — regardless of an English-only system prompt, which is exactly the point: a prompt instruction is a request, not a guarantee. The fix is a deterministic regex filter over the CJK Unicode ranges (carefully excluding Devanagari, since Hindi is a real supported input), applied to every output path — streamed and non-streamed, text and voice — so a language derailment never reaches the user or the TTS engine regardless of what caused it.

The general shape, stated directly in the code: pure heuristics and verification passes first, the LLM only for the residue. That is a harder-won position than it sounds — it means treating every LLM claim about its own actions as unverified until checked, which cuts against how naturally these systems read as trustworthy.

Streaming and correctness were in real tension, and the fix admits the compromise

Token-by-token streaming (for perceived latency) and safe tool-calling are awkward together: Ollama's streaming API doesn't cleanly surface tool calls chunk-by-chunk. Rather than build a chunk-level tool-call accumulator, the design makes a per-turn choice before generating anything — a regex heuristic decides whether a message plausibly needs a tool. Plain chitchat streams directly; anything that might need a tool falls back to the existing safe non-streamed loop. The heuristic is deliberately biased toward "might need a tool," because a missed streaming opportunity only costs some perceived latency, while a wrongly-streamed store/reminder turn silently loses data — an asymmetric cost the code states outright as the reason for the bias.

That still left a gap: a streamed reply that turned out to need a store, phrased outside the regex's coverage, would stream a plausible-sounding confirmation with nothing actually saved. The fix layers the same _needs_data_tool verification pass onto the streamed path after the fact — the visible reply stands (it can't be unsent), but if the check says yes, the real tool call still executes afterward, so the data write catches up to what the user was already told happened. The write-up matters more than the fix here: this is a case where a silent gap in a hardening pass was found by extending the same technique to a second code path, not by anticipating it in advance.

Reliability: fail closed, never fail silent

Every health probe in the system is designed to fail closed — a wedged Ollama, a degraded database, a throttled backend all report their real state through /health, rather than looking healthy by default. A resource guardian samples CPU/RAM/VRAM continuously and only throttles after sustained pressure (roughly 45 seconds over a critical threshold, not one noisy spike), releasing only after a longer sustained recovery window — a real hysteresis circuit breaker rather than a single re-checked threshold, specifically to avoid flapping.

The audit's own framing captures the design philosophy precisely: a flight recorder (BootsLog) exists, but at the time of the audit it only instrumented the wake-word path — typed chat, continuous voice, sync and recall emitted zero events. That's flagged as the single highest-value finding, not because it caused a bug directly, but because it made every other bug un-diagnosable after the fact. Observability is treated as a prerequisite for reliability work, not an afterthought to it.

The audit as a design artifact

The audit itself is worth describing as an architectural choice, not just a QA pass. Five personas, each specifically scoped to a different failure axis — data layer, silent failures, throughput, distributed-systems reliability, coroutine concurrency — reviewed the same shipped codebase independently, explicitly forbidden from changing anything during the review. That separation is what let three different agents converge on the same real bug (the wake-word hang) from three different angles, each describing a different piece of the mechanism. A single reviewer looking for "bugs" in general would likely have found one of the three and stopped there, believing it fixed.

The layer below goes through what those five agents actually found, what's now fixed and device-verified, what's still open, and the specific measured numbers behind the performance claims — including the one where the pre-audit hypothesis about the bottleneck turned out to be wrong.
SDE.lld:
The wake-word hang: three bugs, one symptom

This is the finding worth walking through in full, because no single one of the three defects would have explained the reported symptom on its own, and the audit's whole value was in surfacing all three from independent angles rather than stopping at the first plausible cause.

R-SEV1 (SRE persona): the voice WebSocket client was built with readTimeout(0) and no ping interval. A mid-turn Wi-Fi flake, an access-point handoff, or the laptop suspending (all real, observed conditions on this exact setup) leaves the TCP connection half-open — no FIN, no RST — so OkHttp never fires onFailure or onClosed, and the code waiting on the next socket event awaits forever. The already- written recovery logic (a reconnect-once path, an on-device fallback) was dead code against this specific failure, because it only fires on a closed-socket event that never arrives. The fix was one line — a 10-second ping interval — restoring the existing recovery rather than writing new recovery.

K-SEV1 ×2 (Kotlin-concurrency persona): independently, the streaming microphone's release was fire-and-forget — a bare cancel() on a sibling coroutine, not awaited, so the code that opens the next microphone session had no guarantee the previous one had actually released the hardware. Worse, two of the streaming session's error-exit branches (server error, socket closed) returned without releasing the mic at all — only the "clean finish" and "exception" branches did. A mid-turn failure could leave one microphone still recording while a fallback path opened a second one, which on this hardware produces a documented Android audio-stack silencing behavior (two live AudioRecord instances silence each other).

The merged finding: a dropped connection mid-turn (R-SEV1's exact trigger condition) would land on exactly the error branches K-SEV1 identified as leaking the microphone, at the same moment the half-open socket meant no recovery code would ever run to clean it up. Three findings, one root incident, discovered independently and only combined in the write-up — which is the argument for running five personas rather than one generalist review.

Correctness in the data layer: a silent-loss class, closed at the root

The database-optimizer persona's central finding, cross-referenced against the actual code (db.py): a background write path held a SQLite write transaction open across the agent's own multi-step LLM tool-calling loop — which can span multiple concurrent HTTP round-trips to the model, each taking up to two minutes. Every other background writer (telemetry, the resource guardian's periodic sample, a proactive nudge scan) ran on its own separate connection, and — because they all wrapped their own writes in a broad exception handler — a lock collision with SQLite's default zero-millisecond busy timeout failed instantly and invisibly. A background write could be silently dropped by an unrelated request that happened to be mid-generation.

The fix, read directly from the source comment explaining the decision: autocommit (isolation_level=None) plus WAL mode plus a 5-second busy timeout — chosen deliberately as the fix that removes the entire deadlock/contention class, rather than adding a retry or a lock around the one call site that happened to get noticed. The tradeoff is named explicitly: autocommit means no multi-statement write is atomic anymore, which the design accepts because every write in this schema is independent and the one place that writes multiple related rows (sync) is already idempotent (last-write-wins), so a crash mid-sequence self-heals on the next resync rather than corrupting state. That's the right way to spend a tradeoff — accepting a real, named cost in exchange for eliminating a whole bug class, rather than pretending the cost doesn't exist.

Measured, not estimated: two real performance numbers, and one honest reversal

GPU offload. Ollama's own automatic memory-fit left part of the 4.7 GB Q4_K_M model on CPU (an 18/82 CPU/GPU split), measured at 25.5 tokens/sec on real /chat calls. Forcing full offload with explicit num_gpu=999 confirmed 100% GPU via ollama ps and lifted throughput to 37.3 tokens/sec — a measured +46%, not a benchmark-suite number, from the actual serving path.

Voice latency, and the hypothesis that turned out wrong. Before measuring, the working assumption was that a fixed 1-second silence-detection window before ending a voice turn was the dominant latency cost. A real device capture (Samsung S24, correlated turn-by-turn between the phone's own diagnostics export and the backend's telemetry, matching within 5-20 ms per turn — itself a check that the instrumentation on both ends agrees rather than merely being internally consistent) showed something different: speech-to-text transcription itself was consuming roughly 75% of an 18.6-second average turn, about six times the cost of reply generation and speech synthesis combined. The silence window the original hypothesis targeted could save at most ~300 ms against that — noise against a multi-second stage.

The capture also surfaced its own confound rather than hiding it: the backend had started under genuine memory pressure (RAM at 99%, confirmed via the OS's own counter), and its resource guardian's own log showed it force-unloading the LLM mid-session as a direct consequence. The write-up states the honest caveat explicitly — the direction of the finding (transcription dominates, not the silence window) is trustworthy, since whisper's measured compute time alone was 5-10x its own documented baseline on this exact hardware, but the exact magnitude should be treated as an upper bound until re-measured on a resource-normal machine. Reporting a real number alongside its real confound, rather than laundering it into a clean headline figure, is the standard I'd want this project judged against everywhere else too.

What's fixed, what's open

Twelve of nineteen audit findings are fixed and device-verified as of this write-up, including the wake-word hang cluster above, the WAL fix, a watchdog gap where Ollama could die independently of the FastAPI process it hosts inside without being restarted, and a main-thread I/O stall on the phone's very first frame (five background managers were being started synchronously during initial composition, including a first-time WorkManager database open). Seven remain open, each still carrying its original severity label rather than being quietly downgraded — including the instrumentation gap (typed chat and continuous voice still don't emit the same diagnostic events the wake path does) and a client-side health check that only inspects the LLM's status field, so a database or disk-degraded backend can still report green to a "test connection" button on the phone.

What I'd change

  • Extend flight-recorder coverage to typed chat, continuous voice, sync and recall — the audit's own highest-value finding, still open, and the one that makes every other future bug harder to diagnose for as long as it stays open.
  • Re-run the voice-latency capture on a resource-normal machine to separate how much of the 18.6-second figure is memory-pressure-induced versus an intrinsic floor for whisper-small on this CPU.
  • Fix the client health check to reflect the backend's full top-level status rather than the LLM component alone, so "test connection" can't read green while recall or storage is silently degraded.
  • Keep running the audit periodically rather than treating it as a one-time pass — the wake-word cluster is proof that a single-lens review would have stopped at whichever of the three bugs it found first, and called the symptom fixed.

SDE.name: Rig Animation Pipeline
SDE.description: A headless 2D rig-animation pipeline that turns a topic into a finished cartoon episode — script, voice timing, shot direction, rendered MP4, thumbnail and metadata — with a web console and three human review gates. Built as our own engine rather than paying per-credit for a hosted tool, on the premise that a generative model should supply pixels and never structure.
highlights: Built a four-package TypeScript monorepo (17,135 lines) implementing a headless 2D rig-animation pipeline: a shared rig contract, a job-queue orchestrator with dependency-aware partial re-runs, a rig-agnostic animation engine with an ffmpeg renderer, and a zero-dependency web console with staged review gates.

Designed and versioned the rig contract that makes rigs interchangeable — 29 bones across 7 body-plan archetypes, 8 visemes, 12 expressions, 12 gestures and 4 camera angles as named controls, so the Director drives an auto-generated rig and hand-authored art identically. Carried it through 4 breaking revisions with a changelog explaining what each break was for.

Established the architectural rule the project kept re-deriving: generative image models are unreliable at structure and adequate at pixels, so geometry locates parts via connected-component analysis and a vision model only names them — after an earlier design that asked the model to locate parts proved unusable.

Wired a spend guardrail with per-episode and monthly caps before any generation code existed, and recorded the real dollar cost of each art experiment in the decision log — including $0.36 spent establishing that one sample per prompt is not evidence.

Reviewing it since: the guardrail's ledger is held in memory and left out of the store's disk snapshot, so both spend caps silently reset to zero on restart — one field away from a snapshot that already reasons carefully about not re-spending money on regenerated art.
SDE.overview:
Give it a topic and it produces a finished cartoon episode. The pipeline writes a script, takes recorded narration and measures its real duration, works out the shot-by-shot timing from that audio, animates rigged characters against reusable backgrounds, renders an MP4 with subtitles and music, generates a thumbnail and metadata, and hands the result to a human at three review gates — script, thumbnail, and publish. Everything runs headless behind a web console that shows each stage, its cost, and what it is waiting for.

Why build it rather than use a hosted tool. The commercial options in this space charge per credit, and the format this was built for is deliberately repetitive — the same recurring cast, the same reusable backgrounds, a new episode every few days. That shape rewards owning the engine: characters and backgrounds are generated once and reused forever, and the marginal cost of episode n approaches the cost of narration plus a few AI calls. The tradeoff is that everything the hosted tool does for you is now yours to build, which is what the 17,135 lines are.

The thing worth taking from this project is one rule it kept re-deriving the hard way: a generative image model should supply pixels and never structure. Every attempt to let the model own something structural failed, and each failure narrowed its job:

  • Asking a vision model to locate a character's parts produced boxes that didn't line up. Replaced with connected-component analysis: geometry locates, vision only names.
  • Slicing an assembled figure into parts can't work — a cutout arm hidden behind a torso has no pixels to recover. So characters are drawn already separated, as an exploded sheet of non-touching islands.
  • But an exploded sheet carries no layout information — knowing you have a forearm doesn't say where the elbow sits. So a hand-authored skeleton owns layout and generated art owns only pixels.
  • And structural checks can't catch everything: a face sheet with two mouths passes every structural test there is, because the count of required parts is satisfied.

Cost was treated as a design constraint from the first commit. The spend guardrail — per-episode and monthly caps, with a pre-flight check before every paid call — was wired before any generation code existed. The decision log records the actual dollar cost of the experiments that taught each lesson, including $0.36 spent establishing that one sample per prompt is not evidence. That habit is the part I'd defend most: the numbers are small, but writing them down is what turned prompt work from guessing into something with a cost per unit of knowledge.

The honest status: 13 of 18 phases are shipped and the pipeline runs end to end in the browser, but no episode has been published. Four phases are mid-flight, and the one that matters is the art: the exploded-sheet mechanism is proven and the prompt still does not reliably produce on-model characters. Generated proportions drift from the written style guide and nothing checks them yet. So this is a working machine that is not yet reliably fed — the plumbing, the contract and the cost controls are real; the art stage is still a research problem. Calling it finished would be the easiest lie available here, and the metric on this page says zero for that reason.

No source link: the repository is private.
SDE.hld:
Four packages, one contract, one queue. The shape is conventional; what's load-bearing is the boundary drawn around the generative model, and where each guarantee is allowed to live.

The rig contract is the whole architecture

A rig is any object that exposes an exact set of named controls: 8 visemes for lip-sync, 12 expressions, 12 gestures, 4 camera angles, and the bones for its body plan. One file declares that vocabulary and is the single source of truth — the UI publishes those names to the operator, the auto-rigger builds to them, and an adapter maps hand-authored art onto them.

The payoff is interchangeability: because every rig speaks the same contract, the Director drives any rig identically and rigs can be swapped without touching a line of animation code. An automatically-generated rig and a set of parts drawn by hand and exported as PNGs are, from the Director's point of view, the same thing.

That's a genuine seam rather than a directory that looks like one — the contract file has a version number, a documented changelog, and a validator (missingFromContract) that any importer can run to ask "what is this rig missing for its archetype?" before it enters the pipeline.

Body plans, and the difference between visual and structural decomposition

The contract began implicitly humanoid — two arms with forearms and hands, two legs with feet. That made an animal impossible to rig (a dog on that skeleton is a dog with human arms) and a crowd impossible to represent, and both are recurring cast. So bone requirements became per-archetype: humanoid, four costume variants, quadruped, and group.

The reasoning behind the costume variants is the sharpest thinking in the project, and it turns on a distinction that's easy to get backwards. Two archetypes have bone-identical skeletons and exist anyway, because the costume hides the join; it does not remove the joint. A cutout limb cannot bend unless it is two pieces, so a leg that bends during a walk must be split whether or not the fabric shows a seam there. What the archetype actually selects is which style reference and which costume wording go into the generation prompt — two garments that are drawn completely differently while rigging identically. The archetype is a key into two different tables, and conflating them was a real bug: one garment was classified as a single unbroken drape with no legs at all, and that misclassification is why generation kept returning limbs that could not be split. A wrong domain model in the contract surfaced as an art-generation failure three stages downstream.

The genuinely hybrid case is handled with the same care: a skirt hangs as one piece with no knee to bend, so it gets the single garment bone, while the lower legs below the hem are real articulated parts — and the thigh is deliberately absent, because it is inside the skirt and never visible, so generating it would be asking for art nobody can see. Each simplification is recorded with its cost: a draped shoulder end and long hair are painted onto the torso and head rather than given their own bones, and the price is that neither can move independently.

Where structure is allowed to come from

This is the architectural rule, arrived at by elimination and applied consistently once found: structural guarantees live in code or in a human-authored artifact, never in the model.

  • Layout comes from a hand-authored skeleton file. The skeleton owns where every part sits; the model contributes only the pixels that fill each slot.
  • Part identification is split by reliability: connected-component analysis finds the islands (deterministic, verifiable), and a vision model is asked only to put names to regions it has already been handed. Geometry locates, vision names.
  • Completeness is checked against the contract by code, per archetype, so a rig missing a required bone is rejected at import rather than discovered at render.

The asymmetry in how files are stored follows from the same rule and is called out in the log as load-bearing: part images are cropped to their content, skeleton files are full-canvas. Cropping a part is safe because the skeleton says where it goes; cropping the skeleton would destroy the only copy of the layout.

Cost as a first-class constraint

The spend guardrail exists before the thing that spends. Two caps — per-episode and monthly — with a pre-flight check that must pass before any paid call, and a ledger of actuals afterward. The Director's per-scene loop is careful in a way worth noting: it re-checks the cap before each scene including spend already incurred earlier in the same loop but not yet recorded, so a multi-scene handler can't tunnel through its own cap by deferring its bookkeeping. There's an explicit rule about recording cost in exactly one place to avoid double-counting, and the handlers honour it.

The gap is in durability rather than logic, and it's covered in the layer below.

The queue, and gates as first-class states

The orchestrator is a small in-process queue that replaced a visual workflow tool. Each pipeline stage is a job; a stage that carries a review gate finishes in awaiting_approval rather than approved, so a human decision is a state in the machine and not a convention outside it. The useful piece is dependentsOf: it walks the pipeline's declared dependencies transitively, so changing the script can re-queue exactly the stages that derive from it instead of re-running the whole episode — which matters when re-running costs money.

Two deliberate limits are stated rather than hidden. The in-memory store is documented as swappable for a real queue when scale demands it, with the interface held stable for that purpose. And two stages — script and voice — are manual by design and throw loudly if anything tries to run them automatically, rather than being given a handler that quietly does nothing. Stages that genuinely have no handler yet get an explicit zero-cost placeholder so state transitions stay realistic during development, which is a reasonable choice precisely because the manual-only stages are guarded separately.

A plan overridden on purpose

The console was planned as a React app and deliberately stayed a zero-dependency vanilla JavaScript page, overriding the project's own earlier decision. Show and episode selection persist across a refresh via URL query parameters with no server-side state at all. For a single-operator internal console this is the right trade — but the reason it's worth recording is that the plan was revisited and reversed in writing, with the justification attached, instead of being quietly abandoned.
SDE.lld:
The finding I'd lead with: the spend ledger doesn't survive a restart

The guardrail's design intent is stated at the top of its own file — wired first, before any generation logic, so cost is always controlled. The logic delivers that. The persistence doesn't.

BudgetGuard holds its ledger in a plain in-memory array. The console store persists a great deal to disk on every mutation — shows, episodes, jobs, scripts, voice timings, timelines, and every reference to generated art. The spend ledger is not in that snapshot. The guard is constructed fresh from config on startup with an empty ledger, so monthTotal() returns zero and both caps — including the monthly one, whose entire purpose is to bound cumulative spend across many runs — reset to zero every time the process restarts.

What makes this worth naming rather than just fixing quietly is how close the correct reasoning already is. The snapshot carries a deliberate comment explaining that generated art is the most expensive state in the system, and that leaving it out would mean a restart silently regenerates every rig and re-spends real money. That is exactly the right instinct about restarts and cost — applied to the art, and not to the ledger that counts what the art cost, one field away in the same object.

The fix is small and the data is already there: persisted jobs carry actualCostUsd, episodeId and stage, which is precisely a ledger entry. Rehydrating the guard from the persisted jobs on load — or simply adding the entries to the snapshot — closes it.

Two more spend-path gaps, both in the same shape

  • The cap check is check-then-act with no reservation. canSpend reads the ledger and returns a verdict; nothing is held between that verdict and the later record. Two jobs that both pass the check before either records will both proceed, and the cap is exceeded by design rather than by accident. A reserve-then-settle API — take a hold when the check passes, convert it on completion, release it on failure — is the standard shape and would also give the estimate a place to live.
  • Nothing reconciles an estimate against its actual. The pre-flight check takes an estimated cost and the ledger records the real one. If the actual comes in above the estimate the overshoot is simply recorded after the fact — the cap was checked against a number that turned out to be wrong, and nothing notices or flags the drift. Tracking estimate-versus-actual per stage would both tighten the caps and make the estimates better over time.

The rig contract's changelog is the most valuable file here

Four versions, each with a written justification. The one to read is the split of one draped archetype into four costume variants, because it records a correction rather than an addition: the original mapping treated a pleated male lower garment as a single unbroken drape with no leg bones, which was wrong against the operator's own reference art, and the entry states plainly that this is why generation kept returning un-splittable limbs. Tracing an art-quality symptom back to a type-level misclassification three stages upstream is the kind of finding that only exists if somebody writes the reasoning down as they go.

Two pieces of TypeScript craft support it:

  • as const satisfies readonly Bone[] on each archetype's bone list — keeps the literal tuple types for downstream inference while still validating every entry is a real bone. Getting both at once is the reason satisfies exists.
  • The version note names the intended blast radius: a breaking change to the archetype union means any Record<RigArchetype, T> table fails to compile until its new entries are supplied, and the note calls that the intended safety net. Exhaustiveness is being used deliberately as a migration tripwire rather than merely tolerated.

One thing I'd change: the validator defaults its archetype parameter to humanoid so existing callers keep working. That's a kind default for a refactor and a bad one to keep — a caller that forgets to pass the archetype silently validates a dog against a human skeleton and gets a confident, wrong answer. Now that the callers are migrated, the parameter should be required.

Lessons the log records that generalise past this project

  • Typecheck is not a behaviour test — proved by a literal backspace byte sitting inside a source string, which compiled cleanly and did the wrong thing at runtime. The whole repo's verification story at that point was tsc, and this is the entry that says so out loud.
  • An error message must not assert a cause it cannot know. A review step was reporting a specific reason for a failed split that it had no way to determine, which sends the next reader to the wrong place. Report the observation; leave the diagnosis to whoever has the evidence.
  • A silent fallback must be made loud. Style-reference lookup would fall through to a default when no reference matched, so six added reference files could be ignored with no signal. A reference that matches nothing is now an audible failure.
  • The style guides existed and nothing read them. Written art-direction documents sat in the repo while the image-generation prompts were assembled without them — a documentation artifact that looked like a control and wasn't wired to anything. The same failure shape as a config file nobody loads.
  • Name the wrong outcome, not the category — recorded as recurring three separate times in prompt work: telling a model to avoid a class of mistake is weaker than describing the specific bad result you keep getting.
  • Chroma-key the colour that's actually there, not the one you asked for. The generator was asked for a specific background colour and returned a near-miss, so keying on the requested value left a fringe. Read the real border pixels instead of trusting the request — and separately, a JPEG response breaks single-pixel fringe removal outright, because the compression puts a gradient where the hard edge was.

What's actually unfinished

Stated plainly because the status dashboard does: 13 of 18 phases are shipped, one is untouched, and four are mid-flight. The four matter differently:

  • The art stage is the real blocker. The exploded-sheet mechanism is proven — a live call produced a sheet whose every required bone was a complete, non-touching island — but the prompt does not yet reliably produce on-model characters. Proven mechanism, unreliable output.
  • Generated proportions drift from the written style guide and nothing checks them. Measured and recorded, not yet enforced. A proportion validator against the guide's stated part-to-part ratios is the obvious next control, and its absence is why the art stage still needs a human at every step.
  • Two phases are code-complete but waiting on inputs — hand-authored skeletons and a set of reference-file renames — which is a scheduling gap rather than an engineering one.

What I would change, in order

  • Persist the spend ledger, or rehydrate it from the jobs already on disk. Until then neither cap means what it says across a restart.
  • Make the cap a reservation rather than a check, and record estimate-versus-actual so the estimates can be corrected by evidence.
  • Add the proportion check against the style guide's ratios, so art quality has a programmatic gate instead of resting entirely on the operator's eye.
  • Require the archetype in the contract validator instead of defaulting it to humanoid.
  • Get one episode out. Every remaining uncertainty here is about the art stage under real conditions, and no amount of further plumbing answers it — the pipeline has never been made to produce something someone watched.

3D.name: Taxi Rush
3D.description: A comprehensive taxi driver simulation game featuring real-time ride logic, economic management, and dynamic city navigation.
3D.content:
Taxi Rush is a mobile simulation game that gamifies the daily operations of a ride-hailing driver. It goes beyond simple driving mechanics to simulate the end-to-end service lifecycle, requiring players to manage time, fuel, and earnings within a realistic city economy.

Core Gameplay Loop

The game is built upon a robust GPS State Machine that mimics real-world apps like Uber or Rapido. Instead of just racing, the player engages in a strategic business management loop where every decision—from accepting a Ride Request to managing the Wallet Balance—impacts their ability to continue operating.

How It Works

  • Ride Allocation: A real-time request listener generates "Quest Cards" displaying pickup distance, estimated earnings, and time-to-accept.
  • Verification Logic: The OTP Handshake system forces a physical stop-and-interact moment, ensuring players confirm the passenger before the meter starts.
  • Dynamic Economy: A Surge Pricing System creates Heat Zones on the map, rewarding players for navigating to high-demand areas during rush hours.
  • Financial Constraints: The Wallet Lock mechanism monitors the driver's cash-to-digital ratio, disabling new rides if the commission debt exceeds the threshold.

Key Features & Systems

  • State Management: Distinct logic for Online, Pickup, En-Route, and Payment states
  • User Interface: Realistic notification cards with timers and route previews
  • Incentive Engine: Daily targets and quests to drive player retention
  • Frustration Mechanics: Realistic cancellation scenarios to add emotional stakes
  • Rating System: Post-ride feedback loop affecting driver reputation

This project demonstrates complex state logic implementation, UI/UX design for simulation, and game economy balancing, creating a polished experience that mirrors the real-world gig economy. 🚖
